facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: CodeGrep: 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO to reduce coding agent file exploration overhead
facts.problem: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with a large fraction consumed by grep, glob, and view_file calls during ambiguous exploration loops—often 20+ rounds in wrong directions before the agent gives up.
facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B-parameter retrieval agent built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. It exposes three read-only primitives (regex search, path matching, file contents) mirroring developer navigation. At each turn it emits up to 8 tool calls executed concurrently. During inference, CodeGrep takes the issue description, emits candidate files, and those files are injected into the prompt of a frozen OpenHands downstream agent—only the retriever is trained. Training uses a worktree-based sandbox that replaces Docker images with git worktree add, reducing environment interaction per rollout from minutes to milliseconds. CATM mines 32K samples from 67K open-source agent trajectories (47.7% retention) using GLM-5.1-FP8 as judge model.

evidence.claim: CodeGrep resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified
evidence.condition: 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, temperature 0
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Table 3 / Section 4.3 Downstream evaluation

evidence.claim: Rounds reduction on resolved SWE-Bench instances
evidence.condition: resolved SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep v3 injection
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Table 3 / Section 4.3 Downstream evaluation

evidence.claim: Tokens reduction on resolved SWE-Bench instances
evidence.condition: resolved SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep v3 injection
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Table 3 / Section 4.3 Downstream evaluation

evidence.claim: Precision threshold for retrieval utility
evidence.condition: file-level precision on internal evaluation set, downstream utility regime classification
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 8, Table 2 / Section 5.1 precision threshold analysis

evidence.claim: CodeGrep tool-use efficiency
evidence.condition: average tool-use turns per rollout on internal evaluation set, CodeGrep v3
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Table 2 / Section 4.2 Retriever evaluation

facts.evaluation_context: Evaluation on SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances) using OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as downstream agent, temperature 0, 100-round max. Baseline without retrieval resolves 25.8% at 23.0 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue. Training uses 67K open-source agent trajectories mined via CATM, with GLM-5.1-FP8 as judge model. Training on single 8xB200 node with LoRA, 27-hour wall-clock per run, early-stop at step 897 of 2000-step budget. Environment uses git worktree-based sandbox replacing Docker, enabling per-rollout setup in milliseconds versus minutes. Three-layer architecture extracts unique (repo,commit) pairs, uses git clone --bare and git worktree add for shared object database, and executes grep/glob/read through native subprocesses with 64-way concurrency limit.
facts.limitations: Evaluation limited to SWE-Bench Verified benchmark only—no production deployment data or real-world coding workflows reported. The line-range component was removed because downstream OpenHands editor has no view_range argument, making predicted line ranges dead information at inference time. Training data includes CATM-only entries with no gold line ranges by construction, introducing systematic label bias. The downstream agent is frozen (OpenHands), so results may not generalize to other coding agents like Claude Code. Precision threshold regime characterization based on only three retrievers (BM25, Jina, CodeGrep). End-to-end wall-clock latency not reported, only token and round metrics. Token cost breakdown per tool type (grep vs glob vs read) not reported. Repository index construction cost not explicitly quantified—worktree-based approach described but no specific build time or storage overhead provided. Applying efficiency signal at advantage layer reduces KL drift compared to reward-layer application, but KL still climbs to ~0.02 under v1/v2 before v3 masks only when ¯c>0.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to Agent semantic acceleration focus on reducing repetitive Read, Grep, Glob, and code exploration. CodeGrep demonstrates a clear precision threshold (≈0.45-0.50) below which retrieval degrades downstream agent and above which it buys efficiency. This directly addresses current questions about whether repository indices truly reduce end-to-end task latency—CodeGrep shows 15% rounds reduction and 19% tokens reduction while preserving resolve rate. The work quantifies tool call overhead (2.3 average turns per rollout) and shows retrieval must cross precision ≈0.677 to translate into downstream efficiency. Worktree-based sandbox reduces environment interaction from minutes to milliseconds, enabling single-node training at scale. However, CodeGrep does not address repository index construction cost, false positive rates, error recovery overhead, token cost per-tool breakdown, or whether parallel tool calls introduce correctness risk—limitations that project context specifically asks for.

evidence_gaps.question: What is the token cost breakdown per tool type (grep vs glob vs read) for both CodeGrep and the baseline agent?
What is the overhead comparison between retrieval injection and direct agent exploration in terms of end-to-end wall-clock latency?
What are the repository index construction cost, false positive rate, and error recovery overhead for CodeGrep?

facts.title: Unified Static-Dynamic Pruning for Efficient LLM Inference
facts.event_hint: Research paper presents SPDP, a unified sparse-inference framework for LLM inference
facts.problem: Autoregressive decoding in LLMs suffers from computational and memory bottlenecks. Existing weight pruning methods are confined to either static pruning (permanent but lacks input adaptivity) or dynamic pruning (adaptive but introduces runtime irregularity and coarse-grained masks)
facts.mechanism: SPDP unifies unstructured static pruning with input-adaptive dynamic pruning through co-designed Tiled-Column-wise Bitmap Compressed (Tiled-CBC) format and two GPU kernels: (1) CUDA-core spMspV kernel with Hybrid Activation-aware Dynamic Shared-Memory Bitmap Decoding (HAD-SMBD) for fine-grained activation skipping, and (2) Tensor-Core SpMM kernel for prefill computation. Static and dynamic pruning act on orthogonal dimensions (row-wise vs column-wise), multiplying effective sparsity

evidence.claim: SPDP achieves 1.24x-1.37x average kernel speedup over state-of-the-art SpInfer framework, with maximum up to 2.51x
evidence.condition: Inference-optimized GPUs (A10G, L4), moderate sparsity range 30-50%

evidence.claim: SPDP spMspV kernel achieves 1.88x average speedup over dense cuBLAS baseline on A10G GPU
evidence.condition: A10G GPU, moderate sparsity 30-50% range

evidence.claim: SPDP spMspV kernel achieves 2.11x average speedup over cuBLAS on L4 GPU
evidence.condition: L4 GPU, moderate sparsity 30-50% range

evidence.claim: End-to-end evaluation on LLaMA-2-7B shows SPDP achieves higher average TPOT speedup (×1.34) than SpInfer at comparable sparsity while maintaining lower perplexity (under 5.4)
evidence.condition: LLaMA-2-7B-hf model, end-to-end decode latency measurement

evidence.claim: SPDP achieves higher SM utilization (48.0% vs 38.2-48.0%) and fewer bank conflicts (74 vs 3817) compared to SpInfer
evidence.condition: A10G GPU, (DP, SP) = (30%, 30%) configuration

facts.evaluation_context: Kernel-level evaluation on A10G and L4 GPUs using representative matrix shapes from major LLM architectures (OPT 13B-175B, LLaMA-2 7B-70B, LLaMA-3 8B/70B, Qwen 7B/14B/72B, Mixtral-8×7B, Phi-2/3, gpt-oss). End-to-end evaluation on LLaMA-2-7B-hf model across A10G, L4, and L40S GPUs. Focus on practical sparsity range of 30-50% for both static and dynamic pruning
facts.limitations: Performance gains are constrained by memory-bound nature of decoding workloads and Amdahl-style upper bound from non-sparsity-sensitive operations (attention, normalization). Quantization and unstructured sparsity do not provide multiplicative compression in practice. Evidence limited to moderate sparsity regime (30-60%) typical for large LLMs; extreme sparsity (70-90%) not evaluated as it causes pronounced quality loss in large models
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to AI infrastructure horizontal tracking: addresses GPU kernel efficiency and runtime optimization for LLM serving. Provides concrete system mechanism (unified static-dynamic pruning), performance-per-watt improvements, and engineering boundary (30-50% sparsity range for large LLMs). Should be categorized under 'serving_runtime_compiler' direction

facts.title: SAC: Disaggregated KV Cache System for Sparse Attention LLMs with CXL
facts.event_hint: Research paper presents SAC, the first CXL-based disaggregated KV cache system for sparse attention LLMs
facts.problem: Sparse attention LLMs only utilize a small fraction of KV entries per layer (top-k), but traditional RDMA-based disaggregated memory systems perform coarse-grained full prefix KV cache fetching. This causes two fundamental bottlenecks: (P1) Transmission bottleneck with latency growing near-linearly with concurrency and context length, and (P2) Local memory wasting where only 21% of KV cache is utilized in 128K-context scenarios
facts.mechanism: SAC leverages CXL's cache-line granularity load/store semantics (near-DRAM access latency with zero message protocol overhead) to fetch only required top-k KV entries on demand during inference. Integrates with SGLang HiSparse framework and uses CXL memory pool with multiple CXL-MEM devices interconnected via CXL switch. CXL provides hardware-managed load/store memory semantic at cache-line granularity, achieving remote memory access latencies approaching local DRAM

evidence.claim: SAC achieves 2.1x higher throughput compared to RDMA-based disaggregated memory pool
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 serving, context lengths 16K-128K tokens, integrated with SGLang

evidence.claim: SAC achieves 9.7x lower Time to First Token (TTFT) compared to RDMA-based disaggregated memory pool
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 serving, end-to-end evaluation

evidence.claim: SAC achieves 1.8x lower Time Between Tokens (TBT) compared to RDMA-based disaggregated memory pool
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 serving, end-to-end evaluation

evidence.claim: SAC incurs only 9% throughput degradation compared to non-disaggregated upper bound
evidence.condition: End-to-end serving evaluation

evidence.claim: CXL read latency for sparse KV access ranges from 1.04x to 1.64x of DRAM, while RDMA ranges from 3.97x to 19.7x of DRAM
evidence.condition: Sparse KV cache retrieval with varying number of fetched indices (64-2048)

facts.evaluation_context: Integrated into SGLang serving framework and evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 model end-to-end serving across context lengths from 16K to 128K tokens. System topology includes CXL memory pool with multiple CXL-MEM devices interconnected via CXL switch, PCIe 5.0 x16 links (64 GB/s per link)
facts.limitations: Evaluation limited to DeepSeek-V3.2 sparse attention model; other sparse architectures (GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4) mentioned but not benchmarked. Hardware topology assumes CXL 2.0/3.0 switch availability; deployment constraints in existing datacenters not discussed
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to memory semantics and DSA offloading专题: addresses memory resource disaggregation with new access semantics (CXL load/store at cache-line granularity), demonstrates reduction in memory bandwidth pressure and transmission bottlenecks. Shows end-to-end application benefits (2.1x throughput, 9.7x TTFT). Should be categorized under 'memory_semantics' direction

facts.title: [AAFLOW+] Stateful Operator Abstraction with Zero-Copy Distributed KV Cache Orchestration for Multi-Agent Workflows
facts.event_hint: AAFLOW+: distributed KV cache orchestration system for multi-agent LLM workflows with stateful operators
facts.problem: Multi-agent LLM systems remain fundamentally text-centric, requiring agents to repeatedly recompute shared context through expensive prefill operations. KV-cache management is typically restricted to local serving scopes, limiting reuse across distributed agents.
facts.mechanism: AAFLOW+ extends agentic workflow operators to make KV cache a first-class distributed systems object. It builds processes into communication-aware graphs that concurrently optimize data, prompts, and reusable model state. The system provides operators for KV materialization, transfer, fork, composition, and eviction. Runtime enables zero-copy, transfer-aware execution, allowing agents to reuse long context without recomputation. Forked states initially share block references, so memory grows with branch continuation rather than full-context duplication.

evidence.claim: TTFT reduction on HF backend with Mistral model
evidence.condition: HuggingFace backend, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 model, context grid 1K-32K tokens, mean TTFT

evidence.claim: TTFT reduction on HF backend with Llama3 model
evidence.condition: HuggingFace backend, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct model, mean TTFT

evidence.baseline: SGLang prefix: 1679.81 s (7.63× slower), Dense: 2716.109 s (12.3× slower)
evidence.condition: HF backend, Mistral-7B model, 16 agents, aggregate compute cost

evidence.claim: Multi-agent compute cost reduction at 16-agent scale on HF+Llama3
evidence.baseline: SGLang prefix: 1679.82 s (7.63× slower), Dense: 2303.34 s (10.5× slower)
evidence.condition: HF backend, Llama3-8B model, 16 agents, aggregate compute cost

evidence.claim: Throughput on Mistral with AAFLOW+
evidence.baseline: Dense prefill: 31.94 tokens/s (9.47× slower), vLLM-local: 38.81 tokens/s (7.80× slower)
evidence.condition: Mistral-7B model, generated tokens per second, fixed context grid

facts.evaluation_context: Evaluation uses a trace-driven model parameterized by hardware microbenchmarks on a distributed GPU cluster of 4-16 nodes, each with NVIDIA A100 (80GB/40GB), 32-64 CPU cores, and RDMA-enabled InfiniBand interconnects. Experiments use deterministic synthetic long-context prompts with context lengths from 1K-32K tokens (mean context grid variation), 64 generated output tokens per branch, and agent counts from 1-16. Tested across HuggingFace, vLLM, and SGLang backends with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct models. Network configuration: 25 GB/s (200 Gbps) bandwidth, 50μs network latency for main experiments; Experiment 3 sweeps bandwidth from 10-400 Gbps with both RDMA-like (10μs) and Ethernet-like (100μs) latency settings. TTFT measured at 0.041s (Mistral) and 0.030s (Llama3) for AAFLOW+ vs 2.057s and 0.509s for AAFLOW-text baselines. Throughput measured at ~302 tokens/s vs ~31-40 tokens/s for baselines.
facts.limitations: Evaluation methodology uses analytical cost modeling parameterized by hardware microbenchmarks rather than direct end-to-end runtime measurements on live serving infrastructure. Workloads use deterministic synthetic prompts rather than real-world datasets or production workloads. Validation covers only specific backends (HF, vLLM, SGLang) and models (Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B). Output length is fixed at 64 tokens per branch; TTFT advantage would diminish for longer outputs where decode time dominates. Results are projected from a trace-driven model—the aggregate latency values represent modeled workload costs, not observed Slurm wall-clock runtime. Framework overhead Ω is explicitly modeled as 0.0075s for AAFLOW+, distinguishing orchestration cost from compute. P95 latency, tail behavior, and real serving deployment metrics not reported. Network-side mechanisms that actively perceive KV state placement, inference stages, or token performance goals are not introduced—system operates at distributed systems layer rather than network layer.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to TPN's focus on KV-cache-aware network and bandwidth scheduling. The transfer/recomputation scheduler provides concrete decision rules for when KV transmission outperforms recomputation across different bandwidth conditions (10-400 Gbps). At 200 Gbps with RDMA-like latency, KV transfer is beneficial for most tested contexts; at 10 Gbps, transfer remains preferable for 5/8 contexts. However, AAFLOW+ does not introduce network-side mechanisms that actively perceive KV state placement, inference stages, or token performance goals—it operates at the distributed systems layer rather than the network layer. The work demonstrates that moderate-to-high bandwidth networks make KV transmission superior to recomputation, with specific throughput gains (~302 vs ~32 tokens/s, 7.8-9.5× improvement) and TTFT reductions (0.041s vs 2.057s, 50.2× for Mistral). Framework overhead is explicitly modeled at 0.0075s versus 11.17s for text-based passing. The trace-driven modeling approach distinguishes between orchestration overhead and compute cost, but P95 latency, tail behavior, and real serving deployment metrics are not reported.
